objections.title: The ROI Doesn't Pencil Out
surface: The payback period is too long.
It doesn't make financial sense.
objections.rootCause: Customer calculating the battery as a standalone purchase. The ESS program income changes the math entirely.

disc.D: Wants the bottom line.
disc.I: Responds to excitement about what the battery enables.
disc.S: Doesn't respond to ROI. Lead with peace of mind.
disc.C: Has run their own numbers. Needs ESS factored in specifically.

objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'Before we talk ROI, there's a Connecticut program that changes the math, let me show you that first.'
objections.ctContext: Standard Powerwall 3 earns ~$930/year, ~$9,300 over 10 years. Grid edge: ~$1,755 enrollment vs ~$405.
objections.standardResponse: Before we talk about the financial case, there's a Connecticut state program that actually pays you for owning the battery, and it changes the math significantly. Let me walk you through that first.
objections.repFailure: Engaging in a ROI debate without introducing the ESS program.

extras.DISC: C has run their own numbers and needs ESS factored in specifically. D wants the bottom line. S doesn't respond to ROI, so lead with peace of mind. I responds to excitement about what the battery enables.

objections.title: I'll Add the Battery Later
surface: That's a big number on top of solar.
Can we just do solar first?
objections.rootCause: Battery introduced as an add-on after solar price landed. Retrofit costs materially more than bundling.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'Adding it later isn't the same cost, here's why.'
objections.standardResponse: Adding the battery now versus later isn't the same cost. The crew is already here, the electrical work is already happening. The incremental cost is lower than a separate project. And the ESS program rates aren't guaranteed to stay at current levels.
objections.repFailure: Accepting 'I'll add it later' without explaining the retrofit cost difference.

objections.title: I Don't Lose Power That Often / Don't Need Backup
surface: The grid is pretty reliable here.
We can handle a day without power.
objections.rootCause: Rep led with backup as the pitch. Customer's real motivation is savings or self-supply. This is the most common battery coaching gap. Homeowners rank savings and self-supply first; reps pitch backup first.
objections.technique: Hot Potato. 'Totally fair, backup isn't the only reason. What matters more to you, the savings piece or having the backup?' Then follow their answer.
objections.standardResponse: Totally fair, backup isn't the only reason people go with battery. A lot of our customers add it for the savings piece, storing solar energy during the day and using it at night instead of pulling from the grid at peak rates. And then the ESS program pays you directly from the utility for 10 years on top of that. Is savings and self-supply something that matters to you?
objections.repFailure: Doubling down on backup after the customer has already rejected it.

objections.title: The Utility Controlling My Battery Doesn't Feel Right
surface: I don't want them taking my power.
What if I need it during an event?
objections.rootCause: Misunderstanding of ESS dispatch rules. The actual rules are reassuring, deliver them with confidence.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'Your backup reserve is always protected, the utility cannot touch it.' Then the five rules.
objections.standardResponse: Walk through all five dispatch rules. The backup reserve protection is the key reassurance.
responseDetails: Events only between 12 PM and 9 PM.
Backup reserve always protected (default 20%, utility cannot touch this).
Customer can opt out of any event through the app, no financial penalty.
objections.repFailure: Being vague. The backup reserve protection is the key reassurance.

extras.Master notes: 1. Events only between 12 PM and 9 PM 2. ~24 hours advance notice 3. ~3 hours per event 4. Backup reserve always protected (default 20%, and the utility cannot touch it) 5. Customer can opt out of any event through the app, no financial penalty

variants.rootCause: Misunderstanding of ESS dispatch rules. The actual rules are reassuring, so deliver them with confidence.
variants.standardResponse: Walk through all five. "Events happen between noon and 9pm, with about 24 hours notice, for roughly 3 hours. Your backup reserve, which we set at 20% by default, is always protected. The utility cannot touch it. And you can opt out of any individual event through the app with no penalty."

objections.title: I Need to Talk to My Spouse First
surface: My husband isn't home.
We make big decisions together.
My partner needs to be here.
objections.rootCause: Legitimate stakeholder gap. How the rep handles the present partner determines go-back success.

disc.D: Uses it as an exit formality.
disc.I: Schedules the go-back and does nothing to prepare.
disc.S: Uses it as a shield.
disc.C: Genuinely requires both.

objections.technique: Read the Room on whether the concept is sold. If not, sell the concept before leaving. Then coach the go-back.
objections.ctContext: The 80% Rule: if you don't sell the present partner on the concept before leaving, they cancel 80% of the time. Sell why solar, why Trinity, why now, to whoever is there. Then set a hard return with both present.
objections.standardResponse: Name the absent partner. 'Before I go: when you talk to [name] tonight, what do you think will matter most to them? Let me make sure you have the right answer for whatever they ask.' Schedule the go-back with both confirmed present. Coach them on the one thing [name] will probably care about most.
responseDetails: 'What do you think your spouse is going to like about this?'
'Don't try to sell them before I get back. Just make sure they'll let me in.'
objections.repFailure: From real notes: 'Girlfriend owns the house and I couldn't meet her. He was hard to create urgency with.' Concept not sold to present partner. No coaching language used. Go-back had no purpose.

extras.DISC: D uses it as an exit formality. I schedules the go-back and does nothing to prepare. S uses it as a shield. C genuinely requires both.
extras.Standard response (strong): Coach the present homeowner. Name the absent partner. "Before I go, when you talk to [name] tonight, what do you think will matter most to them? Let me make sure you have the right answer for whatever they ask." Schedule the go-back with both confirmed.
extras.The 80% rule: If you don't sell the present partner on the concept before leaving, they cancel 80% of the time. Ask: "What do you think your spouse is going to like about this?" Then: "Don't try to sell them, just make sure they'll let me in."
extras.Rep failure pattern (real data): "Girlfriend owns the house and I couldn't meet her. He was hard to create urgency with."

objections.title: We Never Decide on the First Appointment
surface: We don't sign on the same day.
We always sleep on big decisions.
objections.rootCause: Stated process preference. Either genuine or polite avoidance. Find out which.

disc.D: Rarely says this. Probe directly.
disc.I: Uses it as a social escape.
disc.S: Most likely. Conflict avoidance as a rule.
disc.C: If genuine, respect it and make the go-back structured.

objections.technique: Hot Potato to determine genuineness. 'That's smart. What questions do you need answered before moving forward?'
objections.standardResponse: That's smart. What questions do you need answered before moving forward? Let's make sure the go-back has a specific purpose. Frame it as a signing appointment, not a review. Every go-back needs: a specific date, a specific time, both decision-makers confirmed, and a stated purpose.
objections.note: This is often a diagnostic signal, not an objection. If the real concern is unstated, probe before leaving.
objections.repFailure: From real notes: 'Believes it makes sense but doesn't sign anything same day.' Go-back scheduled with no named purpose. No stated concern surfaced.

extras.DISC: I uses it as a social escape. S most likely, conflict avoidance as a rule. C: if genuine, respect it and make the go-back structured.
extras.Rep failure pattern (real data): "Believes it makes sense but doesn't sign anything same day."

variants.rootCause: Stated process preference, either genuine or polite avoidance. Your job is to find out which.
variants.standardResponse: "That's smart. What questions do you need answered before moving forward? Let's make sure the go-back has a specific purpose." Frame it as a signing appointment, not a review. Every go-back needs a date, time, both decision-makers confirmed, and a stated purpose.

objections.title: We'd Like to Think About It
surface: We need to process this.
Let us sleep on it.
We'll reach out.
objections.rootCause: This is never about time. It is always one of two things: (1) lack of trust, or (2) incomplete discovery, something undiscovered and hidden. A stall without a named concern is a deferred failure.

disc.D: Rarely says this. Probe directly.
disc.I: Gets vague and friendly.
disc.S: Most common user. Real concern unstated.
disc.C: Has a specific concern not yet voiced.

objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer to acknowledge, then Hot Potato to diagnose. 'Of course, what's the main thing on your mind right now?'
objections.ctContext: Every month of delay = $300-$800 extra paid to Eversource. Name it specifically, once, without pressure.
objections.standardResponse: Ask directly: 'Is it the program, the company, the timing, or something I haven't addressed?' The answer tells you whether it's trust or discovery. Then address the actual root. If trust: don't sell the product harder. Address why Trinity, why this rep. Feel/Felt/Found. Third-party validation. If discovery: something wasn't surfaced. Ask the next question. 'What would need to be true for you to feel confident moving forward today?'
objections.note: Prevention: if you get this at the closing appointment, the first visit wasn't set up correctly. Always open with: 'Nobody is committing today. My job is to make sure everything makes sense. If it's a win-win, great. If not, no problem.'
objections.repFailure: From real notes: 'She needs to process this, one week.' / 'He'll think about it, three weeks.' Both left without the rep naming the real concern or distinguishing trust from discovery.

extras.DISC: D rarely says this, so probe directly. I gets vague and friendly. S is the most common user, real concern unstated. C has a specific concern not yet voiced.
extras.Prevention: If you get this at the closing appointment, the first visit wasn't set up correctly. Always open with: "Nobody is committing today. My job is to make sure everything makes sense. If it's a win-win, great. If not, no problem."
extras.Rep failure pattern (real data): "She needs to process this (one week)." / "He'll think about it (three weeks)." Both left without naming the real concern.

variants.rootCause: Almost never about time. This is an information or trust gap in disguise. A stall without a named concern is a deferred failure.
variants.ctContext: Every month of delay = $300-$800 extra paid to Eversource. Name it specifically.
variants.standardResponse: "Of course. What's the main thing on your mind right now? Is it the program, the company, the timing, or something I haven't addressed?" Then: "What would need to be true for you to feel confident moving forward today?"

objections.title: Not Interested
surface: Not interested.
We're all set.
objections.standardResponse: This is a reflex, not an objection. "Totally get it, I'd probably say the same thing. Takes 60 seconds, fair enough?"

objections.title: I Don't Have Time
surface: We're busy right now.
Not a good time.
objections.standardResponse: "I hear you. 60 seconds to see if it's worth your time later, fair enough?"

objections.title: It's Too Expensive
surface: That's a lot of money.
I wasn't expecting that number.
That's way out of our budget.
objections.rootCause: The rep presented a number before establishing value. Financial objections after pricing are symptoms of thin discovery.

disc.D: Says it bluntly.
disc.I: Goes quiet or changes subject.
disc.S: Says 'let us think about it.'
disc.C: Asks how it was calculated.

objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer, then monthly reframe.
objections.ctContext: At 26-30¢/kWh, the monthly comparison is the only frame that works. Know their actual bill before presenting any number.
objections.standardResponse: Never defend the price. Reframe to monthly. 'You're already paying Eversource $X a month with no ceiling. We're talking about replacing that with $Y and locking it in.' Move to financing only after the monthly frame lands.
objections.repFailure: Jumping to discounting or financing before establishing the monthly comparison.

extras.DISC: D says it bluntly. I goes quiet. S says "let us think about it." C asks how it was calculated.

objections.title: I Can't Afford It Right Now
surface: We're tight right now.
Not in the budget.
Maybe in a year or two.
objections.rootCause: Information gap. The homeowner doesn't realize PPA means no capital outlay. They're replacing a bill, not buying something.

disc.D: Rarely says this.
disc.I: Uses it as a soft exit.
disc.S: Uses it as avoidance.
disc.C: May mean it literally.

objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. One sentence: 'There's nothing to buy.' Then explain.
objections.standardResponse: There's no cost to get started. We're not asking you to buy anything. We're talking about replacing your Eversource bill with a lower number starting the day your system turns on.
objections.repFailure: Jumping to financing before the bill-replacement frame is established.

extras.DISC: D rarely says this. I uses it as a soft exit. S uses it as avoidance. C may mean it literally.

objections.title: I Don't Want Another Bill
surface: I don't need another monthly payment.
We're trying to simplify.
objections.rootCause: Customer sees solar as additive, not a replacement.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. One sentence reframe, done.
objections.standardResponse: You're not adding a bill, you're replacing one. Your Eversource usage charges go away and get replaced with a lower solar payment.
objections.repFailure: Treating this as a financing conversation. It's a one-sentence reframe.

objections.title: Another Company Was Cheaper
surface: Can you do better?
SolarCo quoted me lower.
What's your best price?
objections.rootCause: Trust gap or comparison shopping. Immediately dropping price signals: (1) the original price wasn't justified, (2) we're afraid of losing you, (3) price is the only value.

disc.D: Asks directly. Respond with equal directness.
disc.I: Will mention the competitor seemed friendlier.
disc.S: Won't raise it directly.
disc.C: Compares specs and warranty, not just price.

objections.technique: Be Proactive where possible. Walk-Around Close is the structured response.
objections.standardResponse: The Walk-Around Close has four moves: acknowledge, differentiate, inspect, reframe.

responseDetails.label: Acknowledge.
responseDetails.text: 'Every project is unique and I can't speak to what they may or may not be including.'

responseDetails.label: Differentiate.
responseDetails.text: 'We prioritize transparency. We don't want to call you three months from now with a structural issue that wasn't in the price.'

responseDetails.label: Inspect.
responseDetails.text: 'Let's walk your home together right now: meter, panel, attic. If everything is clean, I'll call my manager and see what we can do.'

responseDetails.label: Reframe.
responseDetails.text: 'I'd rather be honest now than promise a price and come back with problems.'

objections.note: Never: drop price immediately, say 'I'll match it,' or say 'they're cutting corners.'
objections.repFailure: Discounting before doing the walk-around.

extras.DISC: D asks directly, so respond with equal directness. I will mention the competitor seemed friendlier. S won't raise it directly. C compares specs and warranty, not just price.
extras.Never: Drop price immediately. Say "I'll match it." Say "they're cutting corners."
extras.Master notes: 1. **Acknowledge:** "Every project is unique and I can't speak to what they may or may not be including." 2. **Differentiate:** "We prioritize transparency. We don't want to call you three months from now with a structural issue that wasn't in the price." 3. **Inspect:** "Let's walk your home together right now: meter, panel, attic. If everything is clean, I'll call my manager and see what we can do." 4. **Reframe:** "I'd rather be honest now than promise a price and come back with problems."

objections.title: The Numbers Don't Work / Not Enough Savings
surface: The savings aren't that impressive.
I was hoping to save more.
objections.rootCause: Savings presented generically, not against this homeowner's actual bill.
objections.technique: Hot Potato. 'What would make it worth it to you?' Then anchor to their number.
objections.standardResponse: Out of curiosity, what would make it worth it to you? Then calculate against their specific bill. Never present savings without the actual bill in hand.
objections.repFailure: Giving a savings range instead of calculating against the specific bill.

variants.standardResponse: "Out of curiosity, what would make it worth it to you?" Then anchor to their specific numbers. Never present savings without the actual bill in hand.

objections.title: I Need to Run This By My Accountant / Financial Advisor
surface: I want my accountant to look at this.
My financial advisor handles these decisions.
I don't make financial decisions without reviewing them professionally.
objections.rootCause: One of two things: either genuine financial diligence (C-type, high earner, organized) or a polite exit. Determine which before responding.

disc.D: Rarely genuine, more likely avoidance.
disc.I: Unlikely to use this one.
disc.S: Avoidance framed as diligence.
disc.C: Most likely genuine. Welcome it, offer to facilitate.

objections.technique: Hot Potato to determine genuineness. 'That makes sense, what specifically do you want them to review?' If they can name it, it's real. If they can't, it's a stall.
objections.standardResponse: If genuine: 'Absolutely, I can put together a one-page summary with everything they'd need to evaluate this. A lot of accountants appreciate having the numbers laid out clearly. What's the best way to get you back together with both of us on a call?' If stall: 'Of course. What specifically are you hoping they can clarify for you?' Name the concern, address it directly, set a specific go-back with a purpose.
objections.repFailure: Accepting the accountant referral without qualifying whether it's real, then leaving without a committed go-back date and a named question to resolve.

objections.title: I'm Going to Shop Around
surface: I want to shop this around first.
I'm getting a few quotes.
We always compare before we commit.
objections.rootCause: Healthy buying behavior, not a no. Welcome it out loud, then move the comparison off price and onto the things no competitor matches. If you flinch, you've told them the only thing worth comparing is the number.

disc.D: Wants to know fast why you're different, in one line.
disc.I: Shops on who they liked, give them a story they'll repeat.
disc.S: Shopping is the safe, careful move, reassure it's smart.
disc.C: Will build a spreadsheet, hand them the warranty and insurance specifics.

objections.technique: Embrace it, then differentiate. Feel/Felt/Found on the parts a quote sheet never shows.
objections.ctContext: Trinity: 32 years, 125,000+ roofs, BBB A+. The roof penetration warranty runs 25 years where the industry standard is 10. The differentiators are service and the warranty, not the program. Every company offers the program.
objections.standardResponse: I actually love when someone tells me they're going to shop, it means you're taking this seriously, and you should. I'd just ask you to compare more than the number. Every company can quote you the same program. What you can't get everywhere is how we show up after the install. I know how this feels, a lot of my customers felt every quote looked the same on paper, and what they found is the difference shows up the day something needs attention, not the day you sign.
objections.note: Differentiate on white-glove responsiveness, the 25-year roof penetration warranty versus the industry's 10, and the fact that you're a Trinity customer yourself. Compete on what a quote sheet can't show, never on dropping your price.
objections.repFailure: Treating 'I'm going to shop' as a rejection and either folding on price or rushing to a hard close, instead of welcoming it and reframing the comparison onto service and the warranty.

objections.title: The Lowest Quote I Got Is Way Below Yours
surface: Someone quoted me thousands less.
Your price is the highest I've seen.
I can get this done way cheaper.
objections.rootCause: Price conditioning. A homeowner who collected one or two low numbers now believes that's 'the market.' It usually isn't. The low number is often one weak rep on a performance plan, not the company's real price. Every home is custom, so there is no single market price to be below.

disc.D: Throws the number down as a challenge, answer with calm conviction.
disc.I: Repeats what the cheap rep said warmly, don't attack the person.
disc.S: Worried about overpaying, reassure without defending.
disc.C: Has the competing quote in hand, walk the scope line by line.

objections.technique: Don't lose color and don't defend. Reframe what 'the market' even means, then react to the low number with curiosity, not fear.
objections.ctContext: Every roof and system is custom, so identical quotes are a red flag, not reassurance. A price well below the rest is frequently a single under-pressure rep, not a company-wide rate. 90% of roofers are gone within 5 years, and a 25-year agreement is only as good as the company standing behind it.
objections.standardResponse: You wouldn't get three quotes to paint your family portrait and expect them all to be the same, because every one is custom, and your home is the same way. There isn't really one market price to be above or below. Honestly, a number that low usually tells me more about that one rep than about the going rate. I know how that sounds, plenty of my customers felt the lowest quote had to be the best deal, and what they found is the cheapest bid is often the one company that isn't around in five years to honor it.
objections.note: Your reaction is the message. If your face loses color you've told the customer to worry. A calm 'wow, that's a really low price, I'm honestly not sure how they could even offer that' creates doubt the price is even real. Not everybody headed out of business puts up a sign. Never chase the low number to win the moment.
objections.repFailure: Getting conditioned by one or two low quotes, treating them as 'the market,' and either dropping price to chase them or going quiet, which signals the low number is the one to trust.

objections.title: My HOA Won't Allow It
surface: My HOA has rules about this.
I need HOA approval.
objections.rootCause: Most reps don't know CT law. This is the most underused piece of CT-specific knowledge on the team.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'Connecticut law prohibits HOAs from blocking solar.' Then the specifics.
objections.ctContext: Connecticut law (January 2023) prohibits HOAs from blocking rooftop solar without compelling cause. They can regulate placement and appearance. They cannot say no.
objections.standardResponse: Connecticut law actually prohibits HOAs from blocking rooftop solar. They can regulate placement and appearance, but they cannot prohibit installation. Let's get the assessment done so you have the actual design to show them. That's a much stronger position than asking in the abstract.
objections.repFailure: Accepting the objection without citing CT law.

variants.ctContext: Connecticut law (January 2023) prohibits HOAs from blocking rooftop solar without compelling cause. They can regulate placement and appearance, but they cannot say no.

objections.title: I Don't Like the Way Solar Panels Look
surface: The panels look industrial.
I don't want to ruin the look of my house.
objections.rootCause: Image of older blue-silver panels. Doesn't match modern all-black designs.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'The design has changed completely.' Then show, don't describe.
objections.standardResponse: The older panels had a very different look. We use all-black panels now that blend with the roofline significantly better. I can show you installations on homes in your area, the difference is pretty striking.
objections.note: Rule: show, don't describe. Photos of local installations close this fast.

extras.Rule: Show, don't describe. Photos of local installations close this fast.

variants.rootCause: Image of older blue-silver panels, which don't match modern all-black designs.

objections.title: What Happens If I Sell My Home?
surface: We might move in a few years.
What if the buyer doesn't want the panels?
objections.rootCause: Information gap, often masking a buying signal. A homeowner thinking about selling is thinking about home value, which solar supports.
objections.technique: Be Proactive. Raise this before they do if they've mentioned the possibility of moving.
objections.ctContext: Homes with solar sell for 6.9% more (~$25-29K on a median CT home). PPA transfers to the new homeowner.
objections.standardResponse: Solar actually helps you sell. Homes with solar sell for about 6.9% more, roughly $25,000 on a typical CT home. If it's a PPA, the agreement transfers to the buyer easily. Most buyers see it as a feature.
objections.note: Analogy: 'It's like having a pool. If someone doesn't want a pool they probably wouldn't buy that house. Only difference, with a pool you're spending money. With solar, you're saving money.'
objections.repFailure: Using the outdated '20% faster' claim.

variants.ctContext: Homes with solar sell for 6.9% more (~$25-29K on a median CT home). PPA transfers to the new homeowner. "20% faster" is retired.
variants.note: "It's like having a pool. If someone doesn't want a pool they probably wouldn't buy that house. Only difference: with a pool you're spending money. With solar, you're saving money."

objections.title: It's Hard to Sell a House With Solar
surface: I heard solar makes a house harder to sell.
What if a buyer doesn't want to take it over?
Won't the panels scare buyers off?
objections.rootCause: There's a fear underneath this, and it's almost always the very reason to buy. Peel the onion. Every customer means something different by it, so qualify first. The thing they're afraid of, being stuck, is exactly what flips into being protected once you redirect it. Reps resign and treat the fear as the reason they won't buy, when it's the reason they should.

disc.D: Wants the direct value answer, give the sells-for-more number.
disc.I: Picture them showing off the home, lean into the story.
disc.S: Worried about a hard handoff, reassure the transfer is easy.
disc.C: Will want the studies, cite the sale premium and the online-shopping behavior.

objections.technique: Qualify why they're asking first, then reframe with facts. Redirect the fear: same energy, pointed toward the close.
objections.ctContext: Homes with solar sell for about 6.9% more, roughly $25-29K on a median CT home. A PPA transfers to the new owner. The real long-term risk is being the house that can't go solar later if the utility caps interconnection. The '20% faster' claim is retired.
objections.standardResponse: Let me ask what you've heard, because every homeowner means something a little different. Here's what's actually true: solar homes sell for more and quicker. Buyers shop online before they ever visit, so they already know your home has it, and a PPA transfers to them easily. The risk people miss is the other direction, being the house that can't go solar later when the grid fills up. I know it can feel like a thing to explain at sale, a lot of my customers felt the same, and what they found is buyers treat it like a feature, not a hurdle.
objections.note: Standard-feature reframe: 'Would you buy a house without a dishwasher? Nobody passes on their dream house over a $400 appliance, because it's the standard. Twenty years ago it wasn't. That's solar in five years.' Adding it now future-proofs the home.
objections.repFailure: Accepting the surface 'no' and treating the fear as a disqualifier, instead of qualifying what they actually heard and redirecting the fear into the reason to act.

objections.title: What Happens When It Snows?
surface: Does it work in winter?
What about Connecticut weather?
objections.technique: Be Proactive. Raise this before they do, it immediately establishes expertise.
objections.ctContext: Cold temperatures improve panel efficiency. Production estimates are CT-specific, not California figures.
objections.standardResponse: Cold weather actually makes panels more efficient. They produce better in cold than heat. Snow temporarily reduces production but slides off quickly. Panels are warm, black, and angled. Snow clears off them faster than it does off the surrounding shingles. Your estimate is built around CT's actual climate.
objections.repFailure: Vague reassurance instead of leading with the efficiency point.

variants.standardResponse: "Cold weather actually makes panels more efficient. They produce better in cold than heat. Snow temporarily reduces production but slides off quickly. Panels are warm, black, and angled, so snow clears off them faster than it does off the surrounding shingles. Your estimate is built around CT's actual climate."

objections.title: What Happens If I Lose Power?
surface: What good is solar if the grid goes down?
Will solar keep my lights on?
objections.rootCause: Information gap. Without a battery, grid-tied solar shuts off. This is the primary battery conversation opener.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer. 'Without a battery, it shuts off, here's why, and here's what changes with one.'
objections.ctContext: ESS program: Powerwall 3 earns ~$930/year standard, ~$1,395 underserved. Grid edge enrollment: ~$1,755 vs ~$405.
objections.standardResponse: Without battery storage, the system is grid-tied and shuts off during an outage. That's how the utility connection works. That's why a lot of our customers pair it with a battery. And in Connecticut right now, there's a state program that actually pays you for owning one. Want me to walk you through how that works?
objections.repFailure: Stopping at 'it shuts off' without opening the ESS conversation.

objections.title: I'm Waiting for Better Technology
surface: Solar is improving so fast.
Shouldn't I wait?
Won't prices drop?
objections.rootCause: Timing objection disguised as a technology question.
objections.technique: Hot Potato. 'What specifically are you hoping improves?' Then reframe to cost of waiting.
objections.ctContext: Tier 1 panels degrade 0.4-0.5%/year, ~91% output at year 25. Commercial next-gen panels are years from reliability.
objections.standardResponse: Solar always improves, same as a smartphone. But waiting means paying your utility every month in the meantime. A better panel in five years doesn't recover what you paid to Eversource while you waited.
objections.repFailure: Engaging in a technology debate instead of reframing to cost of waiting.

variants.ctContext: Tier 1 panels degrade 0.4-0.5%/year, about 91% output at year 25. Commercial next-gen panels are years from reliability.

objections.title: I Want 100% Offset Or I'm Not Interested
surface: I want it to cover 100% of my usage.
I want my bill to be zero.
If it doesn't wipe out my bill, what's the point?
objections.rootCause: Sizing and expectation gap. Conflates offset with a zero bill, and ignores roof, shading, and program limits.
objections.ctContext: Systems are sized to the roof, shading, and program rules, not always to 100%. The SB4 charge and the small connection fee mean the bill is never literally zero.
objections.technique: Reframe from 'eliminate the bill' to 'lock the part that keeps climbing.'
objections.standardResponse: I get it, the goal is to knock out as much of that bill as possible. We size to your roof and your actual usage, and in most cases we cover the large majority of it. There's still a small connection fee and the state charge, so no honest company can promise a literal zero. What we can do is lock in the part that keeps going up every year.
objections.repFailure: Promising 100% offset or a zero bill to win the moment, then a production shortfall destroys trust.

objections.title: Will Solar Interfere With My Ham Radio / Radio Reception?
surface: I'm a ham operator, won't this wipe out my radio?
I heard SolarEdge kills AM/shortwave reception.
Will the optimizers cause interference on the HF bands?
objections.rootCause: A licensed amateur-radio operator, shortwave listener, or AM hobbyist has heard, often from a forum or club, that SolarEdge systems raise the radio noise floor. The concern is real and documented, so denying it instantly destroys trust with a technical buyer. The move is acknowledge, qualify how exposed they actually are, then route to the known fix.

disc.D: Wants a straight yes/no and the fix, give the levers fast.
disc.I: Reassured by your confidence and track record more than the physics.
disc.S: Worried about hassle, emphasize it's handled and proven.
disc.C: Will engage on the mechanism, walk optimizers, harmonics, ferrites, grounding.

objections.technique: Acknowledge honestly, qualify exposure, then route to mitigation. Never deny it; never promise zero interference.
objections.ctContext: Most homeowners have no HF gear and a short confident answer settles it. The depth only matters for an actual licensed operator running HF from the house.
objections.standardResponse: You're right that some SolarEdge installs have caused interference, it's a real, documented thing, mostly on AM and the HF bands, and only while the panels are making power. Two things put a radio operator at ease: you can shut the system off any time for a contest or an evening net and it goes quiet within seconds, and a standard no-battery system is basically silent at night on its own. And if it ever does interfere, there's a proven fix path, newer optimizers, ferrite chokes, twisted wiring and grounding, that resolves the large majority of cases without removing anything. If you're an active HF operator, I'll flag it on your file so the install team builds the suppression in from the start.
objections.note: Never guarantee zero interference. Promise the process, not perfection. For a serious HF operator, set honest expectations that some mitigation/tuning may be needed.

objections.repFailure: Denying or hand-waving the concern to a technical buyer, or over-promising 'no interference, guaranteed,' instead of acknowledging it and routing to the documented mitigation playbook.

My roof faces the wrong way.

objections.repFailure: Jumping into the pitch as if the prior experience didn't happen. The homeowner who stopped once will stop again with the same trigger.

objections.repFailure: Over-reassuring without explaining the structural protection. 'We've been here 32 years' alone is not a sufficient answer to this question.

objections.title: Why Do You Need My Social Security Number?

disc.S: Quietly uncomfortable, needs gentle reassurance.

objections.title: Do I Still Have to Pay a Utility Bill?
surface: Does solar eliminate my electric bill?
What's my Eversource bill after this?
objections.rootCause: Most customers expect a zero utility bill. The answer is honest and simple. The frame matters more than the number.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer.
objections.ctContext: Solar handles your production. The utility side retains three things: the fixed meter connection fee (~$9.63/month), the SB4 charge on production (3.25¢/kWh, new customers 2026+), and any consumption your system doesn't cover.
objections.standardResponse: Solar covers the usage charges. Those go away and get replaced with your solar payment. On the utility side, you keep a small connection fee, typically about $9.63 a month, and there's a state charge of 3.25 cents per kilowatt-hour on your system's production. We've already factored both into your savings number, so what you're looking at is what you'll actually net.
objections.note: Lead with what solar covers. Mention the utility side as context, not as a warning. Always disclose SB4 before presenting final savings figures.
objections.repFailure: Leading with 'there's a charge' framing rather than 'here's what solar covers.' Or failing to disclose at all, which creates a trust breach when the first utility bill arrives.

extras.Rule: Disclose the non-bypassable charge proactively every time. Never bury it.

objections.title: Natural Gas Will Make Rates Drop / My Expert Says So
surface: My son works in energy and says gas will bring rates down.
Natural gas is cheap, electricity will follow.
Someone in my family does this for a living and told me to wait.
objections.rootCause: An expert in the family, or a confident outside source, has handed the customer a conclusion. The conclusion is the problem, not the person. Concede the person warmly, then contest the conclusion: even if production costs fall, the customer doesn't automatically benefit. Fighting their relative makes you the enemy and them the defender.

disc.D: Wants you to get to the point, give the one-line economist answer.
disc.I: Proud of their smart relative, praise them first.
disc.S: Doesn't want a debate, agree the source is sharp, then redirect.
disc.C: Will engage on the mechanics, walk supply, demand, and the fixed pipeline.

objections.technique: Concede the person, contest the conclusion. Short Answer, Long Answer on why cheaper fuel doesn't reach the homeowner's bill.
objections.ctContext: Production cost and retail rate are not the same line item. A homeowner pays delivery, transmission, and regulated charges layered on top of supply. CT rates have climbed 177% over 25 years (10.9¢ in 2000 to 30.2¢ in 2025) through every kind of fuel market.
objections.standardResponse: Your son sounds like a genius, and I'd trust him on a lot. I may not be a genius, but I look at energy bills all day. Here's the piece that gets missed: even if it gets cheaper to produce power, that doesn't mean you, the homeowner, see it on your bill. You're paying for delivery, transmission, and a stack of regulated charges on top of supply, and those only go one direction. I know it sounds reasonable that cheaper fuel means a cheaper bill. A lot of my customers felt the same after hearing it from someone they trust, and what they found is the production cost dropped before and their rate still went up.
objections.note: Never make the customer choose between you and their relative. Agree the source is smart, then separate 'rates could change' from 'you will benefit.' Those are two different claims.
objections.repFailure: Arguing with the absent expert or dismissing them, which forces the customer to defend their relative instead of hearing the point about who actually benefits.

objections.title: Just Do The Solar, Roof Later
surface: Can we just start with solar?

objections.rootCause: Customer doesn't know the cost of doing it later. Removing and reinstalling solar to re-roof has a real cost, plus material increases, plus mid-project disruption.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer.
objections.standardResponse: If we install solar on a roof near the end of its life, you'll pay twice: once for the new roof, once to remove and reinstall the solar so the roofers can work. The smart move is to bundle now: roofing crew goes first, same project, same financing, same coordination. Plus, if the roof fails after solar, every panel comes off and goes back on. That's a project you don't want to manage twice.
objections.repFailure: Not making the deferred cost concrete. Letting 'I'll do it later' go unchallenged.

extras.Plus: "If your roof fails after solar is installed, every panel comes off, the roof gets replaced, and the panels go back on. That's a project you don't want to manage twice."

surface: What if we move?

objections.rootCause: Almost always a buying signal. They're projecting forward into ownership and resale.
objections.technique: Short Answer, Long Answer.
objections.standardResponse: Yes, with terms. The Trinity craftsmanship warranty transfers once to the next homeowner. The IKO manufacturer side transfers at IKO's discretion, capped at 10 years from original installation. So if you sell in year 3, the new owner gets 7 years of remaining transferred manufacturer coverage on top of your craftsmanship transfer. A new roof is consistently one of the highest-recouped home improvements.

objections.title: It's Still Under Warranty / My Roof Is Newer
surface: The roof was redone before we bought.
It should still be under warranty.
It's only a few years old.
objections.rootCause: Information gap. Most homeowners assume a warranty exists and transfers automatically. It often does not. Manufacturer warranties transfer only once and within a short window after purchase, and many were never registered in the first place.
objections.technique: Hot Potato. Ask for the certificate, then walk the transfer rules.
objections.standardResponse: Good, let's use that. When you bought the house, did they hand you a copy of the warranty certificate? If you have it, that's great, and we'll work around it. Here's the part most people don't know: if there's no certificate, there's a real chance the original contractor never registered it, or it never transferred to you. These warranties usually transfer only once, within about 30 days of the sale. So you may not actually have the warranty you think you have. Let me take a look and we'll find out where you really stand.
objections.note: No certificate usually means no registration or no transfer. Surface it as a question, not an accusation. If they produce a valid certificate, respect it and work around it.
objections.repFailure: Accepting 'it's under warranty' at face value. Not asking for the certificate. Not knowing the transfer-once, short-window rule.
